publications.title: Mass timber compartment fire dynamics simulation with a single-zone model
publications.venue: SiF 2026 – The 14th International Conference on Structures in Fire, Kingston, Ontario, Canada
publications.abstract: This paper describes the validation of a single-zone parametric model to model fire dynamics of mass timber compartments. The use of mass timber in construction is expanding due to its sustainability, embodied carbon, and aesthetic benefits. Unlike conventional noncombustible materials, timber contributes fuel to a fire and changes the fire dynamics and its impact on the structure. Compartment fire experiments provide valuable insights and data related to mass timber compartment fire dynamics. However, limited tests cannot cover the full range of potential design conditions. The cost, scale, and time requirements of such tests also limit the number of tests performed. A simple analytical tool that can reasonably model the fire dynamics of various timber compartments with variations such as compartment geometry, openings, exposed surfaces, and the available fuel contents will be very helpful for design. Validating the model against past experiments allows for its use to help understand the impact of different design choices on fire performance of timber buildings. If necessary, such a simple model can be used to validate more complex and numerically expensive CFD-based fire simulation tools. Single-zone compartment fire models are effective tools to model compartment heat release rate and gas temperatures over time based on the prescribed fuel loads, compartment geometry, and ventilation conditions. However, most existing zone models are built for non-combustible linings and do not explicitly represent the effects of exposed mass timber surfaces, charring, and protection failure. In this work, the single-zone model is extended to account for exposed timber as an additional fuel source, incorporating simplified charring and heat-transfer models to estimate the heat release rate and fuel contribution from timber. The model is implemented in a numerical tool that solves for compartment gas temperature, heat losses, and timber charring depth as a function of time. Validation is carried out in stages, including comparison with OZone for non-combustible configurations, as well as full-scale compartment fire tests for mass timber compartments (e.g., RISE and National Research Council of Canada experiments). Figure 1 shows an example comparison, demonstrating that the model can reasonably reproduce gas temperatures and charring depths over the duration of the fire exposure for different opening factors and timber protection configurations. A parametric study is further conducted to assess the influence of opening size, exposed CLT area, and compartment geometry on compartment temperatures and timber charring depth. The results highlight the sensitivity of compartment fire dynamics to ventilation conditions and the extent of exposed mass timber. The single-zone simulator presented in this work enables rapid evaluation of multiple fire scenarios in mass-timber buildings, offering a practical tool to guide performance-based fire engineering. By efficiently simulating gas temperatures, heat release rates, and charring under different geometries, ventilation conditions, and protection configurations, the model allows engineers to explore design options, optimize fire safety measures, and assess the effectiveness of mitigation strategies before construction. Beyond reproducing known experiments, the framework provides a foundation for future extensions, including structural response modeling, multi-zone fire development, use in conjunction with advanced CFD tools, and integration into probabilistic fire safety analyses.

publications.title: Force-stable reconfigurable truss structures using quadrilateral linkage principles
publications.venue: ASCE EMI Conference 2025 Structural stability student paper competition
publications.abstract: Trusses are valued for their simple design principles and efficient load-bearing capability. However, slow member-by-member assembly and static topology restrict rapid deployment and reconfiguration of trusses for functional use. While mechanical linkages offer rapid deployability and reconfigurability, their scalability for large-scale civil structures is often constrained by the characteristics of their unit cells. These limitations raise the question: Can the design versatility of trusses be combined with the kinematic advantages of mechanical linkages to create structurally efficient, force-stable, scalable, deployable, and reconfigurable systems? To that end, we present a method inspired by flat-foldable quadrilateral linkages to transform static trusses into compactly stowable, reconfigurable systems. An additional node is introduced on the tensile members of triangular units with the help of Grashof linkage principles. This node converts triangles into flat-foldable quadrilateral linkages, enabling system-level reconfigurability while preserving the structure’s load capacity, stiffness and stability. We show that the Fink, Scissor, and Warren trusses can be transformed into reconfigurable systems, achieving up to 93% and 60% reduction in convex hull area and maximum length, respectively, upon actuation of all degrees of freedom. Proof-of-concept prototypes, including a reconfigurable cantilever and a three-meter Warren truss bridge, validate feasibility while demonstrating load capacities and stiffness comparable to their static counterparts. We believe the proposed method will advance the design, analysis and fabrication of sophisticated bar-linked reconfigurable structures with potential applications in deployable infrastructure for aerospace systems, robotic components, metamaterials, and more.
